questions.q: Why isn't a type-valid amount_cents value (e.g., a positive integer) guaranteed to be a correct one?
options: Integers can never be validated by a JSON Schema
input_schema only checks shape (that it's an integer); it says nothing about whether that number actually matches the order's real paid total
The Messages API rejects all integer inputs automatically
Type validity and correctness are the same thing in this context
questions.explain: Schema validation confirms the input matches its declared type and required fields -- it has no way to know whether the value is factually correct, which is why a separate truth check is needed.

questions.q: Where does validate_refund_input run relative to create_pending_approval from Lesson 15?
options: After the reviewer approves the request
Before the pending approval is even created, so a reviewer never sees a request with a bad number
Only after the tool has already executed
It replaces create_pending_approval entirely
questions.explain: Validation runs first -- catching a bad number in code before it's ever escalated to a human means the reviewer's job is reviewing a plausible request, not catching basic arithmetic errors.

questions.q: In validate_refund_input, where does the authoritative paid_total_cents value come from?
options: Claude's tool_use input, taken at face value
The application's own database, via get_order -- not Claude's claim
A hardcoded constant in the validation function
The user's original natural-language question
questions.explain: The lesson's core principle is to re-derive the critical number from your own authoritative source rather than trusting the model's claim, since the model's number could be wrong or manipulated.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend logging rejected and failed-validation cases, not just successful executions?
options: Failed cases are required by the Messages API
They are often more useful than successful entries -- they're the record of every time the system almost did something it shouldn't have
Logging successes alone is illegal
Failed cases take up less storage space
questions.explain: A log of only successful executions can't answer questions about near-misses or repeated problematic requests -- the rejected and failed-validation entries are exactly what surfaces those patterns.

questions.q: What does this lesson say completes the approval checkpoint from Lesson 15?
options: A faster API response time
Input validation (re-verification) and an audit log, together with the pause-before-execute checkpoint
Removing the human reviewer from the loop entirely
A longer tool description with no other changes
questions.explain: Without validation a reviewer could approve a wrong number they had no way to catch, and without logging there's no way to show after the fact that the system behaved correctly -- both layers are necessary, not optional extras.
